title.en: Su Hu Writes 'Never Shall She Enter' on the Palace Wall

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), 16th c. novel, chs. 1-3

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 1-3: the demand for Su Daji, Su Hu's defiant verse, the siege of Jizhou, and the mediation of Ji Chang

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Summoned to court, the border-lord Su Hu refused King Zhou's demand for his daughter — and wrote on the palace wall: 'Never shall I offer my daughter to the wine-soaked king.' The king declared war on Jizhou; the siege broke the town, and the sage King Wen's mediation saved the girl's life — by sending her to the capital after all, where the fox waited on the road.
summary.zh: 紂王索妲己，蘇護題反詩於午門：『冀州蘇護，永不朝商』；崇侯虎征討不克，姬昌修書勸和——護乃獻女入朝，而狐狸候於恩州道上。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The order came that Su Hu's daughter should join King Zhou's palace. The border-lord went to court, heard the demand, and answered with a verse cut on the palace wall: 'Jizhou's Su Hu shall never come to court' — an open declaration of war against the Shang, written in the king's own corridor.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 1-2 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The armies of the north beat at Jizhou's walls until the town starved; then the sage of the west, Ji Chang, sent his letter of mediation, and Su Hu — reading in it the fate of his people — put down the defiance and set his daughter on the road to the capital.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 2-3; not verbatim.

passages.text: The escort reached the post-house of Enzhou at dusk — and there, in the black wind of that night, the fox of Xuanyuan tomb took the girl's body. The rebellion's compromise delivered the kingdom to the fox-queen: a peace that was the beginning of the fall.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 4 transition; not verbatim.

title.en: Yunzhongzi's Wooden Sword Against the Fox

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 5-6

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 5-6: the immortal's wooden sword hung in the Hall of Divinity, the fox's sickness, and the burning of the sword

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The immortal Yunzhongzi, coming down from Mount End-Cloud, saw the demon-qi black over Zhaoge and carved a sword of peachwood for the king to hang in the Hall of Divinity. The fox in Daji's body sickened under it; but the king, told by the 'suffering' consort that the sword was a curse, had the peachwood burned — and the fox-queen, recovered, had Yunzhongzi driven from the city. One sword, burned; six hundred years, ended.
summary.zh: 雲中子見朝歌妖氣，削松木劍懸於分宮樓；妲己（狐）畏劍而病；紂王聽讒焚劍，妖氣復熾——一劍之失，江山傾頹之機。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Yunzhongzi, riding down from the Cloud-End cave, saw a black column of demon-breath standing over the Shang capital, and judged the fall of the dynasty was one fox-deep. He carved a sword of peachwood in a single night and presented it, saying: hang it in the Hall of Divinity, and the evil will burn itself out.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 5 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sword was hung, and the fox in the consort's body lay as if dying, its borrowed skin smoking. The king, weeping at her sickbed, heard her whisper that the wooden blade was a curse meant for the palace — and had it burned in the courtyard.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 5-6, the burning; not verbatim.

passages.text: The fox rose whole, and the immortal was shown the gate. Yunzhongzi went back up the mountain saying one line that the whole novel proves: the mandate of the Shang is over — for when the remedy is burned by the patient, the disease is already the ruler.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 6, the immortal's departure; not verbatim.

title.en: Shen Gongbao, the Recruiter of Every Mountain's Demons

region.en: The roads between Kunlun and the Shang camps (symbolic pin: passes of the west)

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 37 (and throughout)

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 37: Shen Gongbao's defection and his cry of 'Stay, fellow Daoist!'

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Jiang Ziya's own fellow-disciple Shen Gongbao, jealous of the marshal's commission, defected to the Shang with one irresistible skill: wherever he met an immortal, he cried 'Stay, fellow Daoist!' — and talked him into the war. Every beast, god and hermit of the islands came down to die on the Register; the war's whole second act is one man's gift of persuasion, and his head, cut off and thrown to the north wind, still laughs as it flies.
summary.zh: 申公豹妒子牙封神之任，叛而歸商；其所長者一句『道友請留步』——聞者無不反目投商；請來三山五嶽之仙，皆死於封神榜。其頭被砍，拋於北海，猶能飛。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Shen Gongbao had sat forty years on Kunlun beside Jiang Ziya, and when the marshal's commission was given to the other, his jealousy found its weapon: he rode to the Shang camp and offered the fox-queen his services. His art was a single sentence, spoken wherever an immortal walked the roads: 'Stay, fellow Daoist!' — and with the stay began the talk, and with the talk the debt, and with the debt the camp of the Shang. Hermit after hermit came down the mountains to die on the Register of the Investiture, all recruited by one smiling man and one sentence.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 37 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim. / Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 37, the recruiting; not verbatim.

passages.text: The penalty of his treason was written into his own magic: his head, once cut from his shoulders, was flung to the north wind and flew away laughing — a head that could not die, a recruiter who could not stop, a curse on both armies to the last chapter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, the flying head; not verbatim.

title.en: Wen Zhong Dies at Absolute-Dragon Ridge

region.en: Juelong Ridge, on the road home from Xiqi (symbolic pin: Shaanxi passes)

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), ch. 43

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43: the Grand Preceptor's defeat, the prophecy of the character 'Jue', and the fire-pillars of Yunzhongzi

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Wen Zhong, the Grand Preceptor with the golden whip and the ink-black unicorn, had held the Shang together for a lifetime — and his master had warned him long ago of one character: 'Jue,' to cut off. Pursued home from his defeat at Xiqi, he came to a ridge signed with that very name, where the immortal Yunzhongzi waited with eight pillars of spirit-fire; the unicorn fell, the preceptor burned, and the most loyal of the Shang was the first great name carried to the Register.
summary.zh: 聞仲師從金靈聖母，師曾囑『逢絕而止』；兵敗西岐退至絕龍嶺，雲中子以通天神火柱焚之——太師魂歸封神臺，後為雷部之首。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: Wen Zhong, Grand Preceptor of the Shang, rode the ink-black unicorn with the golden pair of whips; his master had warned him once with a single word: wherever the character 'Jue' — to cut off, to end — meets you, turn back.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Defeated at Xiqi, he fled home through the passes and came to a ridge whose stone was signed Absolute-Dragon. Yunzhongzi stood waiting with eight pillars of spirit-fire set around the valley; the pillars rose, the fire closed, and the unicorn and its rider burned where the prophecy had promised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43, the pillars; not verbatim.

passages.text: The soul of the most loyal servant of a doomed house went first to the altar of the Investiture, to be made head of the Thunder Department — the Shang's last pillar turned heaven's own storm-lord, still riding the black clouds that had carried him into every battle.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 43 and the investiture cross-reference; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ten Absolute Formations and Their Ten Sacrifices

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 42-44

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 42-44: the ten formation-masters of the islands and the breaking of each array

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Ten hermit-masters of the islands, recruited by Shen Gongbao, raised ten formations around Xiqi — Heaven-Cutoff, Earth-Fire, Wind-Roar, Ice, Golden Light, Blood-Turn, Flame, Soul-Losing, Red Water, Red Sand — each demanding one mortal sacrifice before its virtue could be matched. The lamp-lighting Patriarch read each formation and fed it a volunteer; ten men went in, ten formations broke — and the broken masters went to the Register, the war's first industrial accounting of souls.
summary.zh: 十位島上散仙擺十絕陣（天絕、地烈、風吼、寒冰、金光、化血、烈焰、落魂、紅水、紅砂）；燃燈道人先以凡人祭陣，破之——十陣十破，陣主皆上榜。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The volunteer-sacrifice mechanic (feeding each formation a mortal) is the novel's most morally stark war-ritual — noted.

passages.text: Ten formation-masters of the islands raised ten arrays before Xiqi, each a pocket of cosmology turned to siegecraft — arrays of cutting heaven, of burning earth, of howling wind, of ice, of golden light, of turning blood, of flame, of losing souls, of red water, of red sand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 42 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Each formation had its law: it could not be broken by force alone until one mortal had fed it — a volunteer walked in and was consumed, and only then could the immortal's counterspell enter. The Patriarch of the Lighting Lamp read each array like an account book, and paid each debt with a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 42-44, the sacrifices; not verbatim.

passages.text: Ten volunteers, ten formations broken, ten masters dead and on the Register: the war's mathematics made explicit. The arrays taught the Xiqi camp its cost, and taught the reader that in the economy of the Investiture, both sides feed the same ledger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 44, aftermath; not verbatim.

title.en: Zhao Gongming, the Black-Tiger God of Wealth, Struck by the Straw Doll

region.en: Emei's Luofu cave and the field before Xiqi (pin: Sichuan–Shaanxi)

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 46-48

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 46-48: Zhao Gongming's descent on the black tiger, his iron whip, and the twenty-one days of the Nailhead Seven Arrows

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Zhao Gongming, the island-god who would become China's God of Wealth, rode down on a black tiger with an iron whip and no bow could touch him — until Lu Ya taught Jiang Ziya the Nailhead Seven Arrows: a straw doll of the god's own shape, shot with an arrow a day for twenty-one days, the last through the heart. The god of riches died of a doll, and his three sisters came to avenge him.
summary.zh: 趙公明騎黑虎執鐵鞭下山助商，鞭傷諸神；陸壓獻釘頭七箭書：草人書名，日射一箭，二十一日而命絕——財神之死，三霄起兵復仇。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The straw-effigy rite is sympathetic magic turned assassination — the novel's most ritual warfare.

passages.text: Zhao Gongming came down from his cave on the back of a black tiger, iron whip in hand, and no weapon of the Xiqi host could touch him; the cloud of his fortune held. So Lu Ya the immortal came to the camp with a book called the Nailhead Seven Arrows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 46-47 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: The rite took twenty-one days: a straw doll cut to the god's own shape, his name written on its chest, an altar raised north of the camp, and one arrow shot into the doll each day at dawn — the first through one eye, the second through the other, and the god on his tiger felt his own body darken with each wound.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 47-48, the straw-doll rite; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the last morning the arrow went through the doll's heart, and Zhao Gongming fell from the black tiger dead. The god of wealth had been killed by a bundle of straw and a book of arrows — and his three sisters, the Ladies of the Three Islands, took up the golden scissors of the flood-dragon to avenge him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 48, the death and the vengeance; not verbatim.

title.en: The Nine-Bends Yellow River Formation: The Sisters Who Scooped Out the Twelve

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 49-50

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 49-50: the three Ladies of the islands, the golden scissors, and the formation that unmade the twelve golden immortals

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The three sisters of Zhao Gongming raised their Nine-Bends Yellow River Formation over the field, with its gates of confusion and its scissors that cut dragons: twelve golden immortals of the Chan sect walked in and walked out stripped of their flower of three openings and their power of nine turns — emperors of the spirit turned to common men. Only the Patriarchs themselves could unmake the formation, and the sisters died on the Register for it.
summary.zh: 三霄娘娘（雲霄、瓊霄、碧霄）為兄報仇擺九曲黃河陣；金蛟剪落十二金仙，削其三花聚頂、閉其胸中五氣；老子、元始親破之——三霄皆上榜。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The three sisters of the islands — Yunxiao, Qiongxiao, Bixiao — raised the Nine-Bends Yellow River Formation for their murdered brother: a maze of nine turns whose gates turned men around, hung with the golden scissors that cut the flood-dragon in two.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 49 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Twelve golden immortals of the Chan teaching walked in to break it, and walked out shorn: the formation scooped from each the flower of three openings and the breath of five powers, leaving them men of no magic — emperors of the spirit, unmade by two women with scissors and a maze.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 50, the unmaking; not verbatim.

passages.text: Only Laozi and the Patriarch Yuanshi could enter it in safety; they broke the maze, took the scissors, and sent the three sisters to the Register — where the ladies of the Yellow River Formation received posts of their own, vengeance and punishment settled in one bookkeeping.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 50, the breaking; not verbatim.

title.en: The Slaying-Immortals Formation of Tongtian Jiaozhu

region.en: The field before the final passes (pin: Shaanxi–Henan)

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 78-79

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 78-79: the Master of the Intercepts' four swords and the four patriarchs who entered the array

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The Master of the Intercepts, humiliated by his sect's losses, hung his four swords of the four gates — Slaying-Immortals, Slaying-Gods, Trapping-Immortals, Ending-Immortals — in a formation that no one being could enter and live. So four came: Laozi, Yuanshi, and the two Buddhas of the west; each took one gate, the swords were pulled, and the formation-master's last argument ended in his own sect's ruin.
summary.zh: 通天教主設誅仙陣，懸誅仙、陷仙、戮仙、絕仙四劍於四門，非四聖不能破；老子、元始、接引、準提各破一門——截教大劫由此而定。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The Master of the Intercepts raised the Slaying-Immortals Formation, one sword hanging at each of the four gates — Slaying-Immortals, Slaying-Gods, Trapping-Immortals, Ending-Immortals — and the law of the array was simple: no single being, however great, could pass any gate alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 78 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: So four came to the four gates: Laozi of the cart, Yuanshi of the seal, and the two Buddhas of the western heaven. Each took one gate and one sword — and where the law required four, four arrived; the swords came down, the gates opened, and the formation that could not be beaten by one was unmade by four.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 79, the four patriarchs; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Master of the Intercepts left the field swearing the final formation — the Ten Thousand Immortals — and the war moved to its last act: a teacher who had lost his array now losing his sect, one sword-debt at a time.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 79, aftermath; not verbatim.

title.en: Bo Yikao's Qin and the Patties Fed to His Father

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 22-23; rabbit variant in later folk layer

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 22-23: the eldest son's embassy, the fox-queen's snare, and the patty of the faithful son

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Bo Yikao, eldest son of the imprisoned King Wen, came to Zhaoge with treasures and a qin to ransom his father; the fox-queen lusted, he refused her, and she had him flayed alive and cooked into patties — which the king was fed, to prove his supposed ignorance. King Wen, who had divined the truth, ate the patties of his own son with a steady face; released, he vomited them on the road, and the three vomited lumps became three white rabbits that bounded into the hills — the folk layer's answer to unbearable grief.
summary.zh: 伯邑考進貢贖父，撫琴而妲己欲私之；邑考不從，被醢為肉餅，以賜文王食之；文王明知而啖之，出羑里吐於地，化為三兔奔入林——兔兒爺之由來（民俗層）。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. Cannibalism-by-trick and the rabbit transformation are the folk layer; handled as recorded narrative, not endorsement.

passages.text: Bo Yikao came down the mountain of his studies to ransom his father from the prison of Youli, bringing the treasures of the west and his own gift: the qin, whose playing drew the birds from the trees and the fox-queen from her chamber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 22 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: She summoned him to teach her the instrument; he refused her with the same courtesy as before, and the refusal was death. The fox had him flayed alive and cooked into three patties, served to the imprisoned king with the words: eat, and prove you know nothing.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 22, the snare and the patties; not verbatim.

passages.text: King Wen, who had divined the whole of it, ate the patties of his own son without a tremor — knowledge swallowed whole — and won his release. On the road home he stopped the carriage, wept, and vomited the three lumps into the grass; the folk layer finishes it: the lumps sprang up as three white rabbits and bounded into the hills, and the moon remembers them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 23, with the folk rabbit variant; not verbatim.

title.en: The Two Princes Sworn to Two Masters

region.en: Zhaoge to Xiqi, the princes' roads (pin: Henan–Shaanxi)

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 11-12 and 60-66

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 11-12 and 60-66: the two sons of King Zhou saved by two immortals, sworn to aid Zhou — and broken by one sentence

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: The two princes of the Shang, sentenced to death by their own father, were snatched from the scaffold by two immortals, trained in the mountains, and sworn to aid Zhou's rise. Shen Gongbao found them with one sentence — 'Your father's throne, and you serve his killers?' — and both broke their oaths: Yin Hong burned in the Taiji diagram, and Yin Jiao, who had sworn to be ground under the plough-heads if he broke faith, was crushed under his own plough of fate — the novel's two cautionary tales of oaths made by the desperate and kept by no one.
summary.zh: 殷郊殷洪臨刑被救，各拜廣成子、赤精子為師，下山時立誓助周伐紂；申公豹一言（『爾父之天下，豈可伐之』）破其誓——殷洪死太極圖中，殷郊遭犁鋤而死，應其誓。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel.

passages.text: The two princes of the Shang, sons of the king who wanted them dead, were taken from the executioner's ground by two immortals of the western teaching and carried up into the mountains — Yin Jiao to the Peak of Jade-void, Yin Hong to the cave of the Red Master.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 11-12 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Each swore at the mountain-gate the oath that released him: to aid the Zhou, to bring down his own father's house. Shen Gongbao met each on the road with one sentence — your father's throne, and you pull it down — and the oath broke: Yin Hong turned his master's teaching into siegecraft and burned in the Taiji diagram for it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 60-66, the broken oaths; not verbatim.

passages.text: Yin Jiao swore the harder oath — that if he broke faith, his body should be ground between the plough-shares — and his oath was kept for him: the prince who died fighting for his father's house was crushed as he had promised, the novel's two mirror-cautionaries of oaths sworn by the desperate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 66, the plough-death; not verbatim.

title.en: Tu Xingsun, the Dwarf Who Dug Through Walls and Was Married by Force

region.en: Jiulong Island and the camps of Xiqi (pin: Shaanxi)

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 53-58

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 53-58: the earth-tunneling of Tu Xingsun, his master's collar, and the forced marriage to Deng Chanyu

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Tu Xingsun, four feet tall and master of the earth-tunnel art, could sink through walls and floors to steal weapons, princesses and battles; he fought for the enemy camp until his own master summoned him by the collar-art and shamed him back to the right side. His dowry was arranged by Jiang Ziya: he was married to Deng Chanyu, the warrior-girl who had beaten him in open field, and died at last in the tunnel-earth under a rival tunneler's rake.
summary.zh: 土行孫身高四尺，擅地行之術，穿牆遁地竊寶劫營；懼留孫以指訣喚之歸周；姜子牙主婚，配鄧嬋玉——最終死於張奎地遁之下。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The forced-marriage arrangement is a novel convention of its period — recorded, not endorsed.

passages.text: Tu Xingsun stood four feet tall and could walk through the earth as through a door: he sank under walls to steal the war-chariots' banners, rose inside tents to cut sentries' throats, and tunneled into the women's towers of the enemy — a soldier whose battlefield was the ground itself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 53-54 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: His master, the immortal Juliuxun, called him home by the finger-sign and shamed him into the Zhou camp — where Jiang Ziya, needing the defector bound by more than loyalty, arranged his marriage to Deng Chanyu, the girl-general whose mace had once knocked him from his mount.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 55-56, the collar and the marriage; not verbatim.

passages.text: He fought the rest of the war from the right side, tunneling for the Zhou — until a rival tunnel-master, Zhang Kui, met him under the earth and killed him in his own element: the digger buried by a deeper digger.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 86-87 cross-reference; not verbatim.

title.en: Yang Jian and the Seven Monsters of Meishan

texts.period: Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen Yanyi), chs. 91-92

source.work: Fengshen Yanyi, chs. 91-92: the seven beast-brothers of Meishan and Yang Jian's transformation-duels

texts.license: Public domain (Ming novel; passages are compiler's renderings)

summary.en: Seven beast-spirits of Meishan — a white ape first among them, with bull, boar, goat, dog, snake and centipede brothers — held the last mountain-pass for the Shang. Yang Jian, the three-eyed god, met them in kind: transformation against transformation, hound against hound, until the white ape Yuan Hong, match of the monkey-kind, was lured into the Mountain-Rivers Painting and roasted in the demon-refining cauldron. The last defenders fell, and the road to Zhaoge lay open.
summary.zh: 梅山七怪（白猿袁洪、豬精朱子真、牛精金大升等）守最後之關；楊戩以七十二變與哮天犬逐之；袁洪入山河社稷圖，斬於陸壓斬仙飛刀——梅山平，兵臨朝歌。

sensitivity.note: Passages are the compiler's condensed paraphrases of the novel. The white ape Yuan Hong is a striking pre-echo of the Monkey King archetype — noted for the trickster cluster.

passages.text: Seven brothers of Meishan held the last mountain for the dying Shang: a white ape, a white ox, a pig, a goat, a dog, a serpent and a centipede, each a spirit of a thousand years in man's shape, each a general in the last army.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 91 (compiler's rendering); not verbatim.

passages.text: Yang Jian met them in their own coin — transformation against transformation, his hound against their beasts — until only the white ape Yuan Hong stood, a fighter of the monkey-kind whose changes matched the god's own and whose head, once cut, regrew.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 92, the duels; not verbatim.

passages.text: The ape was lured into the Mountain-Rivers Painting of the goddess, and there, painted in, was burned in the demon-refining cauldron; the last of the seven fell, the pass opened, and the armies of Zhou came down upon Zhaoge with the war of the gods a chapter from its end.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Fengshen Yanyi, ch. 92, the painting and the cauldron; not verbatim.
